lines.en: What separates fluent speakers from advanced ones is the ability to sound right for every occasion.
It is essential that every candidate be given the same information at the same time.
Were the letter written to a friend rather than a minister, its tone would be entirely different.
However brilliant your idea may be, presenting it in the wrong register can kill it before anyone listens.
The speech, which had clearly been written for academics, left half the audience checking their phones.
Not until you have written the same message in three different styles do you understand what register really means.
Admittedly, 'give us a ring' sounds friendlier than 'contact us', but no company report would ever use it.
It is not what he said that offended the committee, but the way he chose to say it.
Should you require assistance, do ask; but between friends, a simple 'help!' is more than enough.
Rarely does a speaker notice how often they shift register, yet listeners judge them on it every time.
The same request that sounds rude in an email can sound perfectly natural across a kitchen table.
No sooner had he opened his mouth than the whole room knew he had misjudged the occasion.
It is one thing to master grammar, and quite another to know when a casual word fits better than a formal one.
Were the same complaint made in slang, the manager would have laughed; made in legalese, it would have been ignored.
However fluent a speaker becomes, a single wrong register can make them sound like a beginner again.
